## Exercise 2.8

We prove the law of total expectation in the continuous case by using (4), $p(x) = \int p(x,y)\,dy$ and (7), $p(x,y) = p(x|y)p(y)$ from the lecture notes. We work backwards and start from definition of conditional expectation:

\begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}_Y[\mathbb{E}_X[X\mid Y]]
&= \int \mathbb{E}_X[X\mid y]p(y)\,dy\\
&= \int \left(\int x\,p(x\mid y)\,dx\right)p(y)\,dy\\
&= \iint x\,p(x\mid y)p(y)\,dx\,dy\\
&= \iint x\,p(x,y)\,dx\,dy\\
&= \int x\left(\int p(x,y)\,dy\right)dx\\
&= \int x\,p(x)\,dx\\
&= \mathbb{E}[X].
\end{align*}

We then prove the law of total variance by expanding the conditional variance and the variance of the conditional expectation using the variance identity $\operatorname{var}(x) = \mathbb{E}[x^2] - (\mathbb{E}[x])^2$, which follows from expanding the definition (20) in the notes. Starting from the right side and using the law of total expectation from above to the final expression gives:

$\mathbb{E}_y[\operatorname{var}_x(x\mid y)] + \operatorname{var}_y(\mathbb{E}_x[x\mid y]) = \mathbb{E}_y[\mathbb{E}_x[x^2\mid y]] - \mathbb{E}_y[(\mathbb{E}_x[x\mid y])^2] + \mathbb{E}_y[(\mathbb{E}_x[x\mid y])^2] - (\mathbb{E}_y[\mathbb{E}_x[x\mid y]])^2 = \mathbb{E}_y[\mathbb{E}_x[x^2\mid y]] - (\mathbb{E}_y[\mathbb{E}_x[x\mid y]])^2 = \mathbb{E}[x^2] - (\mathbb{E}[x])^2 = \operatorname{var}(x)$

## Exercise 8.9

We look at figure 8.26. The Markov blanket of $x$ consists of its parents, its children and the other parents of its children. We condition on all of these. To show the result with d separation, we have to show that every path from $x$ to a node $y$ outside the blanket is blocked. Such a path has to leave $x$ either through a parent or through a child of $x$. If the path goes through a parent $p$, the arrow goes from $p$ into $x$. This means $p$ is either head to tail or tail to tail on the path. Since $p$ is observed, the path is blocked.

If the path goes through a child $c$, there are two cases. If the path goes $x \to c \to \ldots$, then $c$ is head-to-tail and observed, so the path is blocked. If the path goes $x \to c \leftarrow z$, then $c$ is head-to-head, so $c$ does not block the path. But then $z$ is also a parent of $c$, so $z$ is a co-parent and is observed. The arrow goes out of $z$, so $z$ is head-to-tail or tail-to-tail, and the path is blocked at $z$.

So all paths from $x$ to nodes outside the blanket are blocked, which means
$$p(x | \text{blanket}, \text{rest}) = p(x | \text{blanket})$$
so $x$ is independent of the rest of the graph given its Markov blanket.


## Exercise 8.11

From Section 8.2.1 we have $p(B=1) = 0.9$, $p(F=1) = 0.9$ and

$$p(G=1|B=1,F=1) = 0.8, \quad p(G=1|B=1,F=0) = 0.2$$
$$p(G=1|B=0,F=1) = 0.2, \quad p(G=1|B=0,F=0) = 0.1$$

The driver $D$ only depends on $G$, with $p(D=1|G=1) = 0.9$ and $p(D=0|G=0) = 0.9$. Since probabilities sum to one, $p(B=0) = p(F=0) = 0.1$, $p(D=0|G=1) = 0.1$ and $p(G=0|B,F) = 1 - p(G=1|B,F)$.

First we find $p(D=0|B,F)$ by summing over $G$ and using that $D$ only depends on $G$, so $p(D=0|G,B,F) = p(D=0|G)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
p(D=0|B,F) &= \sum_G p(D=0,G|B,F) \\
&= \sum_G p(D=0|G,B,F)\,p(G|B,F) \\
&= \sum_G p(D=0|G)\,p(G|B,F) \\
&= p(D=0|G=0)\,p(G=0|B,F) + p(D=0|G=1)\,p(G=1|B,F) \\
&= 0.9 \cdot p(G=0|B,F) + 0.1 \cdot p(G=1|B,F)
\end{aligned}
$$

This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
p(D=0|B=1,F=1) &= 0.9 \cdot p(G=0|B=1,F=1) + 0.1 \cdot p(G=1|B=1,F=1) = 0.9 \cdot 0.2 + 0.1 \cdot 0.8 = 0.26 \\
p(D=0|B=1,F=0) &= 0.9 \cdot p(G=0|B=1,F=0) + 0.1 \cdot p(G=1|B=1,F=0) = 0.9 \cdot 0.8 + 0.1 \cdot 0.2 = 0.74 \\
p(D=0|B=0,F=1) &= 0.9 \cdot p(G=0|B=0,F=1) + 0.1 \cdot p(G=1|B=0,F=1) = 0.9 \cdot 0.8 + 0.1 \cdot 0.2 = 0.74 \\
p(D=0|B=0,F=0) &= 0.9 \cdot p(G=0|B=0,F=0) + 0.1 \cdot p(G=1|B=0,F=0) = 0.9 \cdot 0.9 + 0.1 \cdot 0.1 = 0.82
\end{aligned}
$$

If only $D=0$ is observed, Bayes theorem (35) in the notes gives

$$p(F=0|D=0) = \frac{p(D=0|F=0)\,p(F=0)}{p(D=0)}$$

so we need $p(D=0|F=0)$ and $p(D=0)$. For $p(D=0|F=0)$ we sum over $B$, using that $B$ and $F$ are independent, so $p(B|F=0) = p(B)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
p(D=0|F=0) &= \sum_B p(D=0|B,F=0)\,p(B) \\
&= p(D=0|B=1,F=0)\,p(B=1) + p(D=0|B=0,F=0)\,p(B=0) \\
&= 0.74 \cdot 0.9 + 0.82 \cdot 0.1 = 0.748
\end{aligned}
$$

For $p(D=0)$ we sum over both $B$ and $F$, using $p(B,F) = p(B)\,p(F)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
p(D=0) &= \sum_{B,F} p(D=0|B,F)\,p(B)\,p(F) \\
&= 0.26 \cdot 0.9 \cdot 0.9 + 0.74 \cdot 0.9 \cdot 0.1 + 0.74 \cdot 0.1 \cdot 0.9 + 0.82 \cdot 0.1 \cdot 0.1 = 0.352
\end{aligned}
$$

Inserting in Bayes theorem:

$$p(F=0|D=0) = \frac{p(D=0|F=0)\,p(F=0)}{p(D=0)} = \frac{0.748 \cdot 0.1}{0.352} \approx 0.213$$

If also $B=0$ is observed, we use Bayes theorem conditioned on $B=0$. Since $B$ and $F$ are independent, $p(F|B=0) = p(F)$, and we only sum over $F$ in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}
p(F=0|D=0,B=0) &= \frac{p(D=0|B=0,F=0)\,p(F=0)}{\sum_F p(D=0|B=0,F)\,p(F)} \\
&= \frac{p(D=0|B=0,F=0)\,p(F=0)}{p(D=0|B=0,F=0)\,p(F=0) + p(D=0|B=0,F=1)\,p(F=1)} \\
&= \frac{0.82 \cdot 0.1}{0.82 \cdot 0.1 + 0.74 \cdot 0.9} \approx 0.110
\end{aligned}
$$

This is lower than 0.213. The flat battery explains why the driver says the gauge is empty, so the tank does not need to be empty to explain it ("explaining away", as in the slides).

Our model is the graph in Figure 8.54 with $a = B$, $b = F$, $c = G$ and $d = D$.The path $B \to G \leftarrow F$ is head-to-head at $G$, so with nothing observed it is blocked and $B \perp\!\!\!\perp F$. Observing $D$, a descendant of $G$, "unblocks" the path, so $B$ and $F$ become dependent given $D$. This is why also observing $B = 0$ lowers the probability from $p(F = 0 \mid D = 0) \approx 0.213$ to $p(F = 0 \mid D = 0, B = 0) \approx 0.110$, even though $p(F = 0 \mid B = 0) = p(F = 0)$. Since $D$ is only a noisy report of $G$, the first probability is lower than $p(F = 0 \mid G = 0) \approx 0.257$ in (8.32), but the flat battery still explains away the empty reading.


## programming exercise

The model is $y = x^T\theta + \varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon \sim N(0,\sigma^2)$ and prior $\theta \sim N(0, I)$. Since both are Gaussian and $y$ only depends on $\theta$ through a mean shift, $\theta$ and $y$ are jointly Gaussian by (31) in the notes. Conditioning on $y$ with (29) gives the posterior, from Section 4.2 equation (55)-(56) with $\Sigma_\theta = I$:
$$S_N = I - X^T(\sigma^2 I + XX^T)^{-1}X, \quad m_N = X^T(\sigma^2 I + XX^T)^{-1} y$$
The posterior predictive is, by (57) in the notes:

$$p(y|x,D) = N(x^T m_N, \; \sigma^2 + x^T S_N x)$$

The variance is the noise $\sigma^2$ plus $x^T S_N x$, which comes from our uncertainty about $\theta$.

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
set.seed(2026)

grid <- expand.grid(a = seq(-3, 3, length.out = 200), b = seq(-3, 3, length.out = 200))
G <- as.matrix(grid)

run <- function(sx, s2) {
  X <- cbind(rnorm(20, 0, sqrt(sx[1])), rnorm(20, 0, sqrt(sx[2])))
  y <- X %*% c(-1, 1) + rnorm(20, 0, sqrt(s2))
  K <- solve(s2 * diag(20) + X %*% t(X))
  S <- diag(2) - t(X) %*% K %*% X
  m <- t(X) %*% K %*% y
  D <- sweep(G, 2, m)
  grid$pdf <- exp(-rowSums(D %*% solve(S) * D) / 2) / (2 * pi * sqrt(det(S)))
  grid$var <- s2 + rowSums(G %*% S * G)
  print(list(mean = m, cov = S))
print(ggplot(grid, aes(a, b, fill = pdf)) + geom_raster() + coord_fixed() +
        scale_x_continuous(breaks = -3:3) + scale_y_continuous(breaks = -3:3) +
        labs(x = "theta1", y = "theta2", title = "Posterior pdf"))
print(ggplot(grid, aes(a, b, fill = var)) + geom_raster() + coord_fixed() +
        scale_x_continuous(breaks = -3:3) + scale_y_continuous(breaks = -3:3) +
        labs(x = "x1", y = "x2", title = "Predictive variance"))
}
```

## A

This is the case of where $x \sim \mathcal N(0, I)$, $\sigma^2 = 0.1$

```{r, fig.show="hold", out.width="49%", fig.width=4, fig.height=4}
run(c(1, 1), 0.1)
```

The posterior is a small point mass around the true $\theta = (-1, 1)$. The predictive variance is lowest near the origin. It grows about uniformally fast in every direction away from the data.

## D

Now we have $x \sim \mathcal N(0, \operatorname{diag}(0.1, 1))$, $\sigma^2 = 0.1$

```{r, fig.show="hold", out.width="49%", fig.width=4, fig.height=4}
run(c(0.1, 1), 0.1)
```

## Comparison and explanation

In D the posterior is stretched along the $\theta_1$ axis, its variance in $\theta_1$ is roughly 10 times larger than in $\theta_2$, while in A the two are about equal. The predictive variance is also no longer round. It grows faster along the $x_1$ direction than along $x_2$.
This is due to the posterior precision is $S_N^{-1} = I + X^TX/\sigma^2$ (the same as (56), see the remark after it in the notes), and for $N$ points $X^TX \approx N\Sigma_x$. This gives the following for A $S_N^{-1} \approx I + 20 I / 0.1 = \operatorname{diag}(201, 201)$, so we are equally certain about both parameters, Whereas D we have $S_N^{-1} \approx \operatorname{diag}(1 + 20 \cdot 0.1/0.1,\; 1 + 20/0.1) = \operatorname{diag}(21, 201)$.

In D the inputs barely vary in the $x_1$ direction. Changing $\theta_1$ hardly changes the predictions on the training points, so the data says little about $\theta_1$ and it stays uncertain. In the predictive variance, $x^TS_Nx$ is large whenever $x$ points in a direction we have not seen data in (here $x_1$). 

## Changing the label noise to $\sigma^2 = 0.01$

```{r, fig.show="hold", out.width="49%", fig.width=4, fig.height=4}
run(c(0.1, 1), 0.01)
```

With 10 times less label noise, every data point is 10 times more informative. $S_N^{-1} \approx \operatorname{diag}(201, 2001)$.

The posterior is tighter, so on the $[-3,3]^2$ grid it is almost a point, and it sits closer to the true $\theta$. It is still stretched along $\theta_1$, because the shape comes from $\Sigma_x$, not from the noise. The Predictive variance is smaller overall. The floor drops from 0.1 to 0.01, and the $x^TS_Nx$ term shrinks too.






## Exercise 9.10

So we have $p(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{k=1}^K \pi_k\, p(\mathbf{x} \mid k)$ with
$\mathbf{x} = (\mathbf{x}_a, \mathbf{x}_b)$, and assume $p(\mathbf{x}_a) > 0$. Now, for each component we define its marginal and conditional
\[
  p(\mathbf{x}_a \mid k) = \int p(\mathbf{x}_a, \mathbf{x}_b \mid k)\, d\mathbf{x}_b, \qquad
  p(\mathbf{x}_b \mid \mathbf{x}_a, k) = \frac{p(\mathbf{x}_a, \mathbf{x}_b \mid k)}{p(\mathbf{x}_a \mid k)}.
\]
Integrating the mixture over $\mathbf{x}_b$ and as the sum is finite, we can swap sum and integral (fubini), gives
$p(\mathbf{x}_a) = \sum_j \pi_j\, p(\mathbf{x}_a \mid j)$. By the product rule,
\[
  p(\mathbf{x}_b \mid \mathbf{x}_a) = \frac{p(\mathbf{x}_a, \mathbf{x}_b)}{p(\mathbf{x}_a)}
  = \frac{\sum_k \pi_k\, p(\mathbf{x}_a, \mathbf{x}_b \mid k)}{\sum_j \pi_j\, p(\mathbf{x}_a \mid j)}
  = \frac{\sum_k \pi_k\, p(\mathbf{x}_a \mid k)\, p(\mathbf{x}_b \mid \mathbf{x}_a, k)}
         {\sum_j \pi_j\, p(\mathbf{x}_a \mid j)},
\]
which we then write it as
\[
  p(\mathbf{x}_b \mid \mathbf{x}_a) = \sum_{k=1}^K \lambda_k(\mathbf{x}_a)\, p(\mathbf{x}_b \mid \mathbf{x}_a, k)
\]
with
\[
  \lambda_k(\mathbf{x}_a) = \frac{\pi_k\, p(\mathbf{x}_a \mid k)}{\sum_{j=1}^K \pi_j\, p(\mathbf{x}_a \mid j)}
  = p(k \mid \mathbf{x}_a).
\]
This is a mixture distribution. The coefficients fullfill $\lambda_k \geq 0$ and also $\sum_k \lambda_k = 1$,
and each component $p(\mathbf{x}_b \mid \mathbf{x}_a, k)$ integrates to
$p(\mathbf{x}_a \mid k)/p(\mathbf{x}_a \mid k) = 1$ over $\mathbf{x}_b$.
So the mixing coefficients are the responsibilities of the components given $\mathbf{x}_a$, and the
component densities are the conditionals $p(\mathbf{x}_b \mid \mathbf{x}_a, k)$ of the original
components. The coefficients depend on $\mathbf{x}_a$, unlike $\pi_k$.
For a Gaussian mixture, $p(\mathbf{x}_a \mid k) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_a \mid \mu_{k,a}, \Sigma_{k,aa})$
by (2.92) and (2.93), and $p(\mathbf{x}_b \mid \mathbf{x}_a, k)$ is the Gaussian given by (2.81) to (2.82)
with $a$ and $b$ swapped. So the conditional is again a Gaussian mixture.

\section*{Exercise 12.4}

Let $p(\mathbf{z}) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{m}, \Sigma)$ and
$p(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{z}) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{W}\mathbf{z} + \mu, \sigma^2\mathbf{I})$.
This is a linear Gaussian model, so by using (2.115)
\[
  p(\mathbf{x}) = \mathcal{N}\left(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{W}\mathbf{m} + \mu,\;
  \mathbf{W}\Sigma\mathbf{W}^T + \sigma^2\mathbf{I}\right).
\]
A valid covariance $\Sigma$ is symmetric positive definite, so we can write $\Sigma = \mathbf{L}\mathbf{L}^T$
with $\mathbf{L}$ an invertible $M \times M$ matrix. We redefine the
parameters as
\[
  \widetilde{\mathbf{W}} = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{L}, \qquad \widetilde{\mu} = \mu + \mathbf{W}\mathbf{m}.
\]
Then $\widetilde{\mathbf{W}}\widetilde{\mathbf{W}}^T = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{L}\mathbf{L}^T\mathbf{W}^T
= \mathbf{W}\Sigma\mathbf{W}^T$, so
\[
  p(\mathbf{x}) = \mathcal{N}\left(\mathbf{x} \mid \widetilde{\mu},\;
  \widetilde{\mathbf{W}}\widetilde{\mathbf{W}}^T + \sigma^2\mathbf{I}\right),
\]
which is the standard PPCA marginal (12.35)--(12.36) with parameters $\widetilde{\mathbf{W}}$,
$\widetilde{\mu}$ and $\sigma^2$. Since $\Sigma = \mathbf{L}\mathbf{L}^T$ exists for any valid covariance, this works for any $\mathbf{m}$ and $\Sigma$, so assuming $p(\mathbf{z}) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})$ ( should not loose any generality?).

## Programming exercise 2

The VAE has a latent variable $z$ with prior $p(z) = N(0, I)$ and a decoder $p(x|z)$, so $p(x) = \int p(z)\,p(x|z)\,dz$ , as in Section 8 in the notes. Since the pixels are 0 or 1, the decoder gives a Bernoulli probability for each pixel. The encoder approximates the posterior with $q(z|x) = N(\mu(x), \operatorname{diag}(\sigma^2(x)))$, and we train by maximizing the ELBO value $$\mathbb{E}_{q(z|x)}[\log p(x|z)] - KL(q(z|x)\,\|\,p(z)).$$
This is the loss used in the reference example, which we use as a starting point. We load the data with the data loaders from the exercise.

```{python}
import torch
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from torch import nn, optim
from torch.nn import functional as F
from torchvision import datasets, transforms

_ = torch.manual_seed(1)
kwargs = {}

train_loader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(
    datasets.MNIST('../data', train=True, download=True,
                   transform=transforms.Compose([
                       transforms.ToTensor(),
                       transforms.Normalize((0.1307,), (0.3081,)),
                       lambda x: x>0,
                       lambda x: x.float(),
            ])),
    batch_size=128, shuffle=True, **kwargs)
test_loader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(
    datasets.MNIST('../data', train=False, transform=transforms.Compose([
                       transforms.ToTensor(),
                       transforms.Normalize((0.1307,), (0.3081,)),
                       lambda x: x>0,
                       lambda x: x.float(),
                   ])),
    batch_size=1000, shuffle=True, **kwargs)
```

### 1. VAE with a 2 dimensional latent space

We use the model and loss function from the PyTorch example and only change the latent dimension from 20 to 2.

```{python}
class VAE(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super(VAE, self).__init__()
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(784, 400)
        self.fc21 = nn.Linear(400, 2) # here we changed it
        self.fc22 = nn.Linear(400, 2) # again
        self.fc3 = nn.Linear(2, 400) # again
        self.fc4 = nn.Linear(400, 784)

    def encode(self, x):
        h1 = F.relu(self.fc1(x))
        return self.fc21(h1), self.fc22(h1)

    def reparameterize(self, mu, logvar):
        std = torch.exp(0.5*logvar)
        eps = torch.randn_like(std)
        return mu + eps*std

    def decode(self, z):
        h3 = F.relu(self.fc3(z))
        return torch.sigmoid(self.fc4(h3))

    def forward(self, x):
        mu, logvar = self.encode(x.view(-1, 784))
        z = self.reparameterize(mu, logvar)
        return self.decode(z), mu, logvar


def loss_function(recon_x, x, mu, logvar):
    BCE = F.binary_cross_entropy(recon_x, x.view(-1, 784), reduction='sum')
    KLD = -0.5 * torch.sum(1 + logvar - mu.pow(2) - logvar.exp())
    return BCE + KLD


def train(model, epochs=10):
    optimizer = optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
    model.train()
    for epoch in range(1, epochs + 1):
        train_loss = 0
        for data, _ in train_loader:
            optimizer.zero_grad()
            recon_batch, mu, logvar = model(data)
            loss = loss_function(recon_batch, data, mu, logvar)
            loss.backward()
            train_loss += loss.item()
            optimizer.step()
    print('Average loss after {} epochs: {:.2f}'.format(
          epochs, train_loss / len(train_loader.dataset)))


def plot_latent(ax, encode):
    Z, Y = [], []
    with torch.no_grad():
        for data, labels in test_loader:
            Z.append(encode(data.view(-1, 784)))
            Y.append(labels)
    Z, Y = torch.cat(Z), torch.cat(Y)
    points = ax.scatter(Z[:, 0], Z[:, 1], c=Y, cmap='tab10', s=2)
    plt.colorbar(points, ax=ax, ticks=range(10), label='digit')
    ax.set_xlabel('z1')
    ax.set_ylabel('z2')
    ax.set_title('Latent space')
```

```{python}
vae = VAE()
train(vae)
```

### 2. Decoding a grid of latent points

We take $k$ equally spaced values $u$ in $(0, 1)$ and map them through the inverse Gaussian CDF, $z = \Phi^{-1}(u)$. A uniform $u$ gives $\Phi^{-1}(u) \sim N(0, 1)$, so that means the grid points are equally spaced in probability under the prior $p(z)$. We leave out $u = 0$ and $u = 1$, due to that $\Phi^{-1}$ is $\pm\infty$ there. For each of the $k \times k$ grid points we show the mean of $p(x|z)$, that is the pixel probabilities, as a $28 \times 28$ image.

```{python}
def plot_manifold(ax, decode, k=15):
    z = torch.distributions.Normal(0, 1).icdf(torch.linspace(0.05, 0.95, k))
    z1, z2 = torch.meshgrid(z, z, indexing='xy')
    with torch.no_grad():
        imgs = decode(torch.stack([z1.flatten(), z2.flatten()], 1)).view(k, k, 28, 28)
    grid = imgs.flip(0).permute(0, 2, 1, 3).reshape(k * 28, k * 28)
    ax.imshow(grid, cmap='gray', vmin=0, vmax=1)
    ax.axis('off')
    ax.set_title('p(x given z) on a grid')

def plot_vae(encode, decode, title):
    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.5))
    plot_latent(ax1, encode)
    plot_manifold(ax2, decode)
    fig.suptitle(title)
    plt.show()
```

```{python, out.width="100%"}
plot_vae(lambda x: vae.encode(x)[0], vae.decode, 'VAE from the PyTorch example')
```

The left plot shows the encoder mean $\mu(x)$ of each test image, colored by digit. The VAE never sees the labels, but images of the same digit still end up in the same region. The 1s form a separate band, while digits that look alike, like 4, 7 and 9 or 3, 5 and 8, overlap in the middle. The points lie around the origin with roughly unit scale, because the KL term pulls $q(z|x)$ towards $N(0, I)$.

The right plot shows the decoded grid. The digits change smoothly from one to another, and every grid point gives a digit-like image, because the encoded data covers the region where the prior has its mass. Each digit appears in the same place as its cluster in the left plot.
